summary: Pair of range lights (1865) guiding ships through the reefs at Copper Harbor, Lake Superior; the rear light is state-owned and its dwelling is a residence.

structures.type: lantern on keeper's dwelling, replaced by skeletal tower
structures.note: Six-room dwelling built summer 1868 after Congress appropriated $5,000 on 20 July 1868. Skeletal tower replaced the dwelling lantern in 1964 (cite 2).
22-foot wooden tower, 450 feet north of the dwelling. Replaced by a white steel tower on a tank house in 1927 (cite 2).

access.note: Rear light and dwelling owned by the Michigan Historical Museum System. The dwelling houses the assistant manager of Fort Wilkins State Park. Grounds open; dwelling and tower closed; respect privacy (LHF).

facts.agency: Michigan Historical Museum System (rear light, per LHF)

events.note: Congress appropriated $3,500 for range lights to mark the entrance to Copper Harbor (20 June 1860).
Pair of range lights constructed on the Fort Wilkins reservation (LHF; USLHS tower established 1865).
Keeper's dwelling built after Congress appropriated $5,000 on 20 July 1868 (LHF).
Lightning struck the front tower; repaired 1884 and a conductor added (LHF).
Charles T. Davis appointed after William Tresise died in February 1885 (USLHS, LHF).
Main Copper Harbor Lighthouse converted to acetylene and placed under the range keeper (LHF).
Steamer Samuel Mather aground on Gull Rock on 19 October 1923 (LHF). Two men from the disabled steamer reached the station on 20 October (Bulletin).
Keeper Davis's letter describing the close of the 1924 season (printed in the Bulletin early in 1925).
Copper Harbor and Mendota keepers gave food and shelter to shipwrecked sailors and Coast Guard crew (letter dated 31 December 1926).
Wooden front tower replaced by a white steel tower on a tank house (LHF).
Charles H. Haven succeeded Davis, who retired 30 September 1930 (LHF, USLHS).
Range lights electrified, eliminating the need for a resident keeper (LHF).
Skeletal tower replaced the lantern room on the dwelling (LHF; station record gives 1964 for tower 2).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1,376 m spread between records comes from Wikidata's point for the front range (47.4811, -87.8667), which lies about 1.4 km north of the station. LHF places the front tower 450 feet (about 137 m) north of the dwelling. The OSM point (47.46872, -87.86651) fits LHF and is kept.

notes_for_editor: 1) Two separate Copper Harbor stations exist in the sources. This story is the range lights only. The main Copper Harbor Lighthouse (the 1849 light at Fort Wilkins) and its keepers are not written here. Henry Corgan, who served at 'Copper Harbor' per the 1924 Bulletin, is not added because the Bulletin does not say which light. 2) The 1923 Bulletin notice is garbled in the scan: it interleaves two notices. The attributions are read as Davis as keeper, Holman as assistant, the rescue on 20 October, and the keeper's night walk. The page image should be checked before publication. 3) 'George R. Holman' is read from 'Geo rge R. Holman' in the OCR. 4) Whether the range lights still show is not stated in the sources read. USLHS records 'Active Aid to Navigation: No'; the record says 'active' (OSM). LHF says they were electrified in 1937. Check the Coast Guard list of lights. 5) LHF's 1896 newspaper item is second-hand; the newspaper was not checked on Chronicling America. 6) Front tower status today is not given. 7) The 1964 skeletal tower date appears in both the record (Rowlett 'tower 2') and LHF. 8) Charles H. Haven (1930 to 1937) is named; his connection ended in 1937, before the 1960 cut-off. 9) The record's front-range structure gives 'built: null'; LHF's 1865 date for the pair is used. 10) Verification pass (2026-10-28): the 1923 Bulletin notice is interleaved with a notice for another station (the 'dory' and 'Ginn' text). The story no longer quotes the spliced passage about the keeper's night walk; it paraphrases the contiguous words, and says which man was credited with which act is uncertain. 11) The 1925 letter is printed in the Bulletin's 1925 volume (PDF p. 2), not dated more precisely than 1925. 12) The 1926 letter was addressed to the lighthouse superintendent at Detroit (the Bulletin's 1927 notice), not to the keepers; the story says so.
